title: Giving the Proverbial Kick-in-the-Pants Pep Talk
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article offers a specific technique for challenging an underperforming team member without further demotivating them: leading with a genuine affirmation of the person's strengths before making the ask to improve. It contrasts affirming openers ('When you focus, no one is better than you') with negative framings that undercut a person's confidence and invite resistance, arguing that the former is more likely to land as a demand rather than a put-down. The piece closes by locating character not in how the team member responds to tough feedback, but in how skillfully the leader frames the challenge in the first place.
points: Occasionally challenging an underperforming team member directly is a necessary leadership task.
The key technique is opening with a genuine affirmation before making the performance ask.
Affirming openers make a challenge feel demanding rather than demeaning.
Negative framings that undercut a person's strengths tend to trigger resistance and discouragement.
The article argues leadership character shows up in how the challenge is framed, not just in the team member's response.
quotes: Every once in a great while, an unmotivated team member requires a swift kick in the backside to reenergize their focus.
The key is to begin the message by underlining a strong belief in the team member BEFORE making the appeal to improve.
When a challenge begins with affirmation, it is more likely to be viewed as demanding as opposed to demeaning.
Your raw brain power is heads and tails above everyone else.
Beginning with a negative frame will likely result in resistance and discouragement.
The truth is, character is most in play with how the leader frames the challenge.
It takes a strong and principled leader to offer a positive challenge.
